# On the Peculiar Joy of Small Discoveries

I've been thinking about how the best moments in life often arrive unannounced, wearing no special outfit.

Yesterday I found a coffee shop I'd walked past a hundred times but never entered. Inside, afternoon light pooled on wooden tables, and an old woman was reading in the corner with the focused intensity of someone truly lost in a book. I ordered something I'd never tried, sat by the window, and watched people navigate the sidewalk below. Nothing remarkable happened. And yet.

There's something about small discoveries that feels subversive in our age of optimization. We're encouraged to research everything exhaustively beforehand—read the reviews, check the ratings, know what you're getting into. But there's a particular kind of aliveness that comes from stumbling into something unknowingly, from letting surprise back into your day.

I think this extends beyond coffee shops. We've outsourced our serendipity to algorithms, and they're perfectly efficient at giving us more of what we already want. But what we actually need is more randomness, more wandering, more willingness to waste time—which isn't wasted at all, just unmonetized.

The woman with the book glanced up and smiled at nothing in particular. I wondered if she'd discovered this place intentionally or by accident. I wondered if it mattered.

On my walk home, I took three wrong turns. Found an alley I'd never seen, noticed flowers blooming in an unexpected color. Got delightfully lost for twenty minutes in my own neighborhood.

Some of the best parts of living aren't about arrival. They're about the path you take by accident.
